[[Image:Tubular neighborhood.png|right|thumb|A curve, in blue, and some lines perpendicular to it, in green. Small portions of those lines around the curve are in red.]]
[[Image:Voisinage tubulaire.svg|right|thumb|A close up of the figure above. The curve is in blue, and its tubular neighborhood ''T'' is in red. With the notation in the article, the curve is ''S'', the space containing the curve is ''M'', and <math>T = j(N).</math>]]
[[Image:Tubular neighborhood3.png|right|thumb|A schematic illustration of the normal bundle ''N'', with the zero section <math>N_0</math> in blue. The transformation ''j'' maps ''N''<sub>0</sub> to the curve ''S'' in the figure above, and ''N'' to the tubular neighbourhood of ''S''.]]
In [[mathematics]], a '''tubular neighborhood''' of a [[submanifold]] of a [[smooth manifold]] is an [[open set]] around it resembling the [[normal bundle]]. The tubular neighbourhood deformation retracts onto the submanifold.

The idea behind a tubular neighborhood can be explained in a simple example. Consider a [[Smooth function|smooth]] curve in the plane without self-intersections. On each point on the [[curve]] draw a line [[perpendicular]] to the curve. Unless the curve is straight, these lines will intersect among themselves in a rather complicated fashion. However, if one looks only in a narrow band around the curve, the portions of the lines in that band will not intersect, and will cover the entire band without gaps. This band is a tubular neighborhood. 

In general, let ''S'' be a [[submanifold]] of a [[manifold]] ''M'', and let ''N'' be the [[normal bundle]] of ''S'' in ''M''. Here ''S'' plays the role of the curve and ''M'' the role of the plane containing the curve. Consider the natural map
:<math>i : N_0 \to S</math>
which establishes a [[bijective]] correspondence between the [[zero section]] <math>N_0</math> of ''N'' and the submanifold ''S'' of ''M''. An extension ''j'' of this map to the entire normal bundle ''N'' with values in ''M'' such that <math>j(N)</math> is an open set in ''M'' and ''j'' is a [[homeomorphism]] between ''N'' and <math>j(N)</math> is called a tubular neighbourhood.

Often one calls the open set <math>T = j(N),</math> rather than ''j'' itself, a tubular neighbourhood of ''S'', it is assumed implicitly that the homeomorphism ''j'' mapping ''N'' to ''T'' exists.

== Normal tube ==

A '''normal tube''' to a [[Smooth function|smooth]] curve is a [[manifold]] defined as the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of all discs such that
* all the discs have the same fixed radius;
* the center of each disc lies on the [[curve]]; and
* each disc lies in a plane [[Orthogonality|normal]] to the curve where the curve passes through that disc's center.

== Formal definition ==

Let <math>S \subseteq M</math> be smooth manifolds. A tubular neighborhood of <math>S</math> in <math>M</math> is a [[vector bundle]] <math>\pi: E \to S</math> together with a smooth map <math>J : E \to M</math> such that
* <math>J \circ 0_E = i</math> where <math>i</math> is the embedding <math>S \hookrightarrow M</math> and <math>0_E</math> the zero section
* there exists some open sets <math>U \subseteq E</math> and <math>V \subseteq M</math> with <math>0_E[S] \subseteq U</math> and <math>S \subseteq V</math> such that <math>J\vert_U : U \to V</math> is a [[diffeomorphism]]. 

The normal bundle is a tubular neighborhood and because of the diffeomorphism condition in the second point, all tubular neighborhood have the same dimension, namely (the dimension of the vector bundle considered as a manifold is) that of <math>M.</math>

== Generalizations ==

Generalizations of smooth manifolds yield generalizations of tubular neighborhoods, such as regular neighborhoods, or [[Sphere_bundle#Spherical_fibration|spherical fibrations]] for [[Poincaré space]]s.

These generalizations are used to produce analogs to the normal bundle, or rather to the [[stable normal bundle]], which are replacements for the tangent bundle (which does not admit a direct description for these spaces).
